 20 Epilogue: The Success of General-To-Specic
                 Model Selection
Preamble
Throughout this book, we have emphasized the essential roles of methodology in the development of sound
econometric models and of computers in making that econometrics operational. The former study has led to the
theory of reduction as a basis for general-to-speciﬁc modelling procedures to build congruent empirical models.
Equally, software packages for data management, graphics, estimation, testing and simulation have underpinned many
of the great strides in the discipline. During the preparation of the present edition, a new generation of computer
programs has appeared which bids fair both to resolve many of the methodological issues about model selection that
have been the subject of debate – by demonstrating that general-to-speciﬁc works – and greatly to reduce the burdens
of empirical modelling. This epilogue explains these important developments and discusses their implications.


1 Introduction
Although many aspects of econometric methodology remain in dispute, there is actually a surprising dearth of
evidence on the performance of any approaches. Recent developments seem set to resolve several of the central
problems. To investigate how well general-to-speciﬁc (Gets) model selection performs in practice, Hoover and Perez
(1999) simulate an operational algorithm and demonstrate that it does well for linear, dynamic regression models in
many cases, despite excessive initial over-parameterization.
Building on their approach of searching many reduction paths, Krolzig and Hendry (2000) have automated Gets in a
program called PcGets, embodying the principles discussed in earlier chapters.1 First, the initial general statistical model
is tested for congruence, which is maintained throughout the selection process by diagnostic checks, thereby ensuring a
congruent ﬁnal model. Next, statistically insigniﬁcant variables are eliminated by selection tests, both in blocks and
individually. Many
468                                           RETROSPECT AND PROSPECT


reduction paths are searched, to prevent the algorithm from becoming stuck in a sequence that inadvertently eliminates
a variable that matters and thereby retains other variables as proxies. If several models are selected, encompassing tests
resolve the choice; and if more than one congruent, mutually encompassing choice remains, model-selection criteria
are the ﬁnal arbiter. Lastly, sub-sample signiﬁcance helps identify ‘spuriously signiﬁcant’ regressors.
PcGets, therefore, implements all of the methodological prerequisites argued for in this book. To give an analogy, PcGets
works like a series of sieves. After testing that the initial model is congruent, it ﬁrst removes the completely irrelevant
variables subject to retaining congruence, then checks all initially feasible reduction paths to remove less obviously
irrelevant variables, before testing between the contending selections by encompassing. The chosen congruent and
encompassing model is then examined by checking the signiﬁcance of variables in sub-samples to see if any ‘fools gold’
remains. In Monte Carlo experiments, PcGets recovers the data-generation process (DGP) with an accuracy close to
what one would expect if the DGP speciﬁcation were known, but nevertheless coefﬁcient tests were conducted.
Empirically, on the DHSY and UK M1 data sets discussed extensively above, PcGets selects (in seconds!) models at
least as good as those developed over several years by their authors. Thus, an operational version of the Gets
methodology conﬁrms its power.
Computer automation of model selection is in its infancy, and already considerable progress has been achieved. The
exceptional progress to date merely sets a lower bound on performance. Moreover, there is a burgeoning symbiosis
between the implementation and the theory – developments in either stimulate advances in the other. This additional
chapter explains the background to the Gets approach, the theory that sustains it, its achievements to date, how PcGets
functions, and why it can perform so well despite the apparent statistical problems. It also shows PcGets in action on
the two main empirical studies in chapters 8–10 and 11–12 respectively, and outlines the exciting prospects offered by
extensions of computer automation to model selection based on sound methodology.
The structure of the chapter is as follows. In section 2 we ﬁrst review, then refute, most of the potential criticisms of
general-to-speciﬁc methods. Section 3 describes the main methodological innovations that have opened the door to
computer automation of general-to-speciﬁc model selection procedures. Then section 4 explains how PcGets
implements the methodology of reduction, discriminating between the costs of inference and the costs of search, and
describes the steps in the algorithm. Section 5 discusses the factors affecting the probability of selecting relevant
variables, and section 6 considers the determinants of the probability of deleting irrelevant variables. Putting these
together in section 7 enables us to explain why PcGets performs so well. Section 8 reports the outcome of applying
PcGets to the two problems most studied above, namely the DHSY and UK M1 models. Section 9 concludes.


2 Potential Criticisms
Critics of general-to-speciﬁc methods (henceforth denoted Gets) have pointed to a number of potential difﬁculties,
including the problems of ‘lack of identiﬁcation’,
                                  EPILOGUE: THE SUCCESS OF GENERAL-TO-SPECIFIC                                          469


‘measurement without theory’, ‘data mining’, ‘pre-test biases’, ‘ignoring selection effects’, ‘repeated testing’, and the
potential ‘path dependence’ of any selection: see inter alia Faust and Whiteman (1997), Koopmans (1947), Lovell
(1983), Judge and Bock (1978), Leamer (1978), Hendry, Leamer and Poirier (1990), and Pagan (1987). Koopmans'
critique followed up the earlier attack by Keynes (1939, 1940) on Tinbergen (1940a, 1940b) (discussed in chapter 1)
and set the scene for doubting all econometric analyses that failed to commence from pre-speciﬁed models. Lovell's
study of trying to select a small relation (zero to ﬁve regressors) hidden in a large database (forty variables) found a low
success rate, thereby suggesting that search procedures had high costs and supporting an adverse view of data-based
model selection. The fourth criticism concerned applying signiﬁcance tests to select variables, arguing that the resulting
‘estimator’ was biased in general by being a weighted average of zero (when the variable was excluded) and an unbiased
coefﬁcient (on inclusion). The ﬁfth concerned biases in reported coefﬁcient standard errors from treating the selected
model as if there was no uncertainty in the choice. The next argued that the probability of retaining variables that
should not enter a relationship would be high because a multitude of tests on irrelevant variables must deliver some
‘signiﬁcant’ outcomes. The sixth suggested that how a model was selected affected its ‘credibility’: at its extreme, we
ﬁnd the claim in Leamer (1983) that ‘the mapping is the message’, emphasizing the selection process over the
properties of the ﬁnal choice. In the face of this barrage of criticism, many economists came to doubt the value of
empirical evidence, even to the extent of referring to it as a ‘scientiﬁc illusion’ (Summers, 1991). Nevertheless, all of
these criticisms are refutable, as the following sections demonstrate, although it is convenient to analyse them in the
reverse order.


2.1 ‘Path Dependence’
The problem of ‘path dependence’ is whether the results obtained in a modelling exercise depend on the simpliﬁcation
sequence adopted, or are unique from any given starting-point. Since the ‘quality’ of a model is intrinsic to it, and
progressive research induces a sequence of mutually encompassing congruent models, proponents of Gets consider
that the path adopted is unlikely to matter. As Hendry and Mizon (1990) expressed the matter: ‘the model is the
message’. Nevertheless, it must be true that some simpliﬁcations lead to poorer representations than others. Hoover
and Perez (1999) turned this problem on its head by proposing to search many feasible reduction paths. Since different
outcomes might eventuate from different paths searched, this suggestion initially leads to a proliferation of choices.
However, all of these are congruent models, so encompassing tests can be used to select the dominant equation.
Consequently, a unique outcome does result, with the property that it is congruent and undominated, resolving any
‘path dependence’ critique. Moreover, to quote from their paper (p. 189):

   The searched speciﬁcation may, nevertheless, possess epistemic virtues not open to the one-shot test: since the
   correct speciﬁcation necessarily encompasses all incorrect speciﬁcations, the fact that the searched speciﬁcation is
   naturally nested within a very general speciﬁcation, which nests a wide class of alternative speciﬁcations in its turn,
   strengthens the searched speciﬁcation as a contender for the place of model-most-congruent-to-the-truth.
470                                           RETROSPECT AND PROSPECT


   The evidence of strength is not found in the t-statistics, but in the fact of the Darwinian survival of the searched
   speciﬁcation against alternatives and in its natural relationship to the general speciﬁcation.

Their re-run of Lovell's Monte Carlo certainly resulted in greatly improved performance – yet it is feasible to
considerably improve upon that, as we will see.


2.2 ‘Repeated Testing’
The theory of repeated testing is easily understood: conducting twenty independent tests at a 5 per cent signiﬁcance
level (i.e. a one-in-twenty risk) when the null is valid should on average lead to one ‘signiﬁcant’ rejection by chance.
Since model selection entails conducting many tests, it may seem that spurious results will surely be obtained with high
probability. In fact, the probability p that none of the tests rejects at 5 per cent is:



Viewed as a type-I error, 1 − p0.05 = 0.64 is large, but even with so many irrelevant tests, on more than a third of the
occasions that twenty are conducted, none will reject. Most of that 0.64 probability is concentrated on one test rejecting
(0.38) with a 19 per cent chance of two, and a 6 per cent chance of three rejects. However, it is difﬁcult to obtain
spurious t-test values much in excess of three despite repeated testing: as Sargan (1981) pointed out, the t-distribution
is ‘thin tailed’, so even the 0.5 per cent critical value is less than three for ﬁfty degrees of freedom. One solution,
therefore, is to use larger critical values. When forty tests of correct null hypotheses are conducted, p0.05 ≃ 0.13, whereas
p0.005 ≃ 0.89. Unfortunately, more stringent criteria for avoiding rejections when the null is true lower the power of
rejection when it is false.
The logic of repeated testing seems impeccable, and indeed is accurate as a description of the statistical properties of
mis-speciﬁcation testing: conducting four independent diagnostic tests at 5 per cent will lead to about 19 per cent false
rejections. Nevertheless, even in that context, there are possible solutions – such as using a single combined test –
which can substantially lower the size without too great a power loss (see e.g. Godfrey and Veale, 1999). It is much less
clear that the analysis is a valid characterization of selection procedures in general. The ideas in Hoover and Perez
(1999) not only make computer automation of model selection practical, they also reveal a hidden assumption in
previous analyses thereof, namely that just one path is searched. Searching just one path is generally detrimental,
because there is no ‘error correction’ for wrong reductions – an early inappropriate decision can lead to an overly large,
yet mis-speciﬁed ﬁnal selection. That difﬁculty may well explain the poor characteristics of ‘step-wise’ regression,
which Leamer (1983) parodies as ‘unwise’. Searching all the feasible paths increases the chances that some will retain
the variables which matter, while eliminating those which do not. In the smaller set that remains, the importance of the
relevant variables should be clearer. In fact, the resulting theory dramatically alters our understanding of the model-
selection problem: the serious practical difﬁculty is not one of avoiding
                                  EPILOGUE: THE SUCCESS OF GENERAL-TO-SPECIFIC                                            471


‘spuriously signiﬁcant’ regressors because of ‘repeated testing’ when so many hypotheses are tested – multiplied many-
fold by all the paths searched; it is one of retaining all the variables that genuinely matter. In general, our models will be
too small, omitting relevant factors that happen not to be ‘signiﬁcant’ in the given sample, rather than too large by
retaining adventitiously signiﬁcant variables (see section 5).


2.3 ‘Selection Effects’
If a wide variety of models would be reported when applying any given selection procedure to different samples from a
common DGP, then the results using a single sample must apparently understate the ‘true’ uncertainty. Coefﬁcient
standard errors only reﬂect sampling variation conditional on a ﬁxed speciﬁcation, with no additional terms from
changes in that speciﬁcation (see e.g. Chatﬁeld, 1995). Thus, it may be felt, one should ‘inﬂate’ reported uncertainty to
reﬂect the fact that models were selected from data evidence. To understand this criticism – and its rebuttal – two
concepts are involved: that of a ‘local DGP’ and that of ‘collinearity’, so we consider these aspects in turn.
From the theory of reduction, there always exists a unique ‘local DGP’ (denoted LDGP) of the variables being
modelled, formally derived from the actual DGP by reduction (see inter alia Hendry, 1995a; Mizon, 1995; Bontemps
and Mizon, 1996). Any economy under study may comprise billions of decisions and millions of recorded variables,
generated by the DGP of agents' behaviour and the recording procedures. The LDGP is the corresponding
representation for the subset of variables under analysis such that, were the LDGP known, the outcomes could be
predicted up to an innovation error. Thus, computer-generated data from the LDGP would differ only randomly from
the actual values, and would do so in the same way as equivalent data generated from the DGP itself. No assumptions
about ‘constant parameters’ or stationary data are needed in justifying this analysis, although highly non-constant
coefﬁcients in any resulting econometric model would render it useless. The implication is that selection must be
judged against the LDGP.
Reported empirical estimates and associated measures of uncertainty can only be judged conditional on accepting the
resulting equation as a good approximation to the LDGP. Undominated (i.e. encompassing) congruent models have a
strong claim to provide such an approximation, and conditional on that, their reported uncertainty is indeed a good
measure of the uncertainty inherent in such a speciﬁcation for the relevant LDGP. Notice that their ‘closeness’ to the
actual DGP does not matter for this argument, albeit that it is crucial in general if econometric models are to be of
practical value. Consequently, the remaining question concerns the reliability with which the same selection will be
made in repeated samples. Surprisingly, this is difﬁcult to determine. To understand which aspects of selection
genuinely increase uncertainty and which are artefacts, we must re-consider ‘collinearity’.
Perfect collinearity denotes an exact linear dependence between variables; perfect orthogonality denotes no linear
dependencies. However, any state in between these is harder both to deﬁne and to measure as it depends on which
‘version’ of a model is inspected. Most econometric models contain subsets of variables that are invariant to linear
transformations, whereas measures of collinearity are not invariant: if two
472                                           RETROSPECT AND PROSPECT


standardized variables x and z are nearly perfectly correlated, each can act as a close proxy for the other, yet x + z and
x − z are almost uncorrelated. Moreover, observed correlation matrices are not reliable indicators of potential
problems in determining whether either or both variables should enter a model – the source of their correlation
matters. For example, inter-variable correlations of 0.9999 easily arise in systems with unit roots and drift, but there is
no difﬁculty determining the relevance of variables. Conversely, in the simple bivariate normal




                                                                                                                    (20.1)
where we are interested in the DGP



                                                                                                                    (20.2)
(for ‘well-behaved’ εt, say), when ρ = 0.9999 there would be almost no hope of determining which variables mattered
in (20.2), even if the DGP formulation were known. In economic time series, however, the former case is common,
whereas (20.1) is almost irrelevant (although it might occur when trying to let estimation determine which of several
possible measures of a variable is ‘best’). Transforming the variables to a ‘near-orthogonal’ representation before
modelling would substantially resolve this problem; otherwise, eliminating one of the two variables seems inevitable.
Of course, which is dropped depends on the vagaries of sampling, and that might be thought to induce considerable
‘unmeasured uncertainty’ as the chosen model oscillates between retaining xt or zt. However, either variable individually
is a near-perfect proxy for the dependence of yt on β xt + γ zt, and so long as the entire system remains constant,
selecting either, or the appropriate sum, does not actually increase the uncertainty greatly. That remains true even when
one of the variables is irrelevant, although then the multiple-path search is highly likely to select the correct equation.
And if the system is not constant, the ‘collinearity’ will be broken.
Nevertheless, the outcome of a Monte Carlo model-selection study of (20.2) given (20.1) when ρ = 0.9999 might
suggest that ‘model uncertainty’ was large – and coefﬁcient estimates badly biased – simply because different variables
were retained in different replications. The appropriate metric is to see how well β xt + γ zt is captured. In some cases,
models are estimated to facilitate economic policy, and in such a ‘collinear’ setting changing only one variable will not
have the anticipated outcome – although it will end the ‘collinearity’ and so allow precise estimates of the separate
effects. The transformation of the variables to a ‘near-orthogonal’ representation before modelling is assumed to have
occurred in the remainder of this chapter. By having a high probability of selecting the LDGP in such an orthogonal
setting, the reported uncertainties (such as estimated coefﬁcient standard errors) in PcGets are not much distorted by
selection effects.


2.4 ‘Pre-Test Problems’
To understand the ‘pre-test’ problem, we must brieﬂy distinguish between the costs of inference and the costs of
search, discussed more fully in section 4.1. Statistical tests are designed to have non-degenerate null distributions, and
hence have non-zero
                                 EPILOGUE: THE SUCCESS OF GENERAL-TO-SPECIFIC                                          473


size and (generally) non-unit power. Consequently, even when the LDGP is known a priori from economic theory, if an
investigator does not know that the resulting model is in fact ‘true’, but seeks to test conventional null hypotheses on
its coefﬁcients, then in general inferential mistakes must occur. These will vary as a function of the characteristics of
the LDGP and of the particular data sample drawn, but for many parameter values the selected model will differ from
the LDGP, and hence have biased coefﬁcients. This is the ‘pre-test’ problem and the associated costs are those of
inference, since no ‘search’ is involved, in the sense that the model is the LDGP and no simpliﬁcation is required.
The costs of search are the additional mistakes introduced by commencing from an initial model that is much larger
than the LDGP. Thus, search costs comprise retaining any irrelevant variables signiﬁcant by chance, as well as omitting
relevant variables, more often than an investigator who began from the LDGP.
The deﬁnition of ‘success’ implicit in this analysis is ‘exactly locating the LDGP’. In economics, this does not seem a
sensible measure, so to judge the ‘success’ of Gets, a different metric is proposed, namely the additional costs of
commencing from an overly large model rather than from the LDGP. This measure does not resolve the ‘pre-test’
problem, but it clariﬁes how much worse empirical research will be by having to search for the relevant variables in a
morass of potential – but actually irrelevant – candidates. Surprisingly, these additional costs are small, as shown in
section 7: PcGets retains relevant variables with probabilities close to those achieved when testing the LDGP, and omits
irrelevant variables most of the time. Of course, such an outcome does not remove the costs of inference, but it does
argue for commencing from a general speciﬁcation that nests the likely LDGP, since doing so has low costs, whereas
the converse of commencing from too simple a speciﬁcation precludes ever locating the LDGP.


2.5 ‘Data Mining’
This pejorative term has many possible meanings, some of which correspond to activities unlikely to be productive of
useful results, and some of which are actually excellent modelling procedures (see e.g. Leamer, 1978; Sargan, 1973;
Hendry, 1995a; Campos and Ericsson, 1999, who distinguish four senses and propose remedies for each). Searching
through ‘literally hundreds of regressions’ (as in Friedman and Schwartz, 1982) for a result that corroborates a prior
theory is a procedure with unknown size and power, but seems almost certain to produce spurious ﬁndings. We call
such an approach, and related activities, ‘weak data mining’. ‘Strong data mining’ occurs when conﬂicting evidence is
deliberately hidden, ignored, or not reported, so is clearly unscientiﬁc. Fortunately, both forms are open to adversarial
scrutiny by checking how well the resulting model encompasses rival studies using the same data set. Strong data
mining fails immediately as conﬂicting evidence already exists by deﬁnition; weak fails when rival models cannot be
encompassed – and if they can, then an undominated model was selected despite the inappropriate procedure. Thus,
stringent critical evaluation renders this criticism otiose. Gilbert (1986) suggests separating the output of any empirical
study into two groups, where the ﬁrst contains only redundant results (those parsimoniously encompassed by the
ﬁnally selected
474                                          RETROSPECT AND PROSPECT


model), and the second contains all other ﬁndings. If the second group is not null, then there has been data mining. On
such a characterization, Gets cannot involve data mining, despite depending heavily on data-basing.
We have already disposed of the repeated testing’ objection (which argues that simply conducting multiple tests will
induce signiﬁcant outcomes by chance), of the ‘selection’ problem (that the uncertainty in the reported results may not
reﬂect the true uncertainty in the study), and of the ‘collinearity’ problem (selecting variables that chance to be
correlated with the relevant factors).
On the positive side, productive data mining requires a procedure that has a high probability of locating the LDGP. In
Monte Carlo, such an attribute can be checked, since the DGP itself is known: methods which do badly in such a
setting seem unlikely to do well in empirical research. Structured searches, such as those embodied in PcGets, can have
low search costs and perform well in simulation experiments, suggesting that ‘data mining’ may end up being a
compliment.


2.6 ‘Measurement Without Theory’
‘Measurement without theory’ has long been an insult capable of virtually dismissing empirical work from serious
consideration. There are two main strands, deriving respectively from the criticisms by Keynes (1939, 1940) of
Tinbergen (1940a, 1940b), and from those by Koopmans (1947) of Burns and Mitchell (1946).
In chapter 1, I expressed the worry that the criticisms of Tinbergen by Keynes remained unrebutted. Keynes had
claimed a number of ‘preconditions’ for the validity of inference from data, including a complete prior theoretical
analysis, with all relevant phenomena measurable, explanatory variables which represented independent inﬂuences,
pre-selected lag length, choice of variables and trend, and time homogeneity (or parameter constancy). In Keynes's
view, Tinbergen's work did not satisfy such preconditions, so he scornfully dismissed it (see the many quotes in chapter
1). In retrospect, we can see that Keynes held to an extreme form of the ‘axiom of correct speciﬁcation’ (see Leamer,
1978), namely that statistical work in economics is impossible without knowledge of everything in advance. If partial
explanations were devoid of use, and if empirically we could discover nothing not already known, then no science
could have progressed. This is clearly refuted by the historical record. Given my discussion in the Preamble to chapter
2, I am surprised it took me so long to understand the fallacy in Keynes's argument: since theoretical models are
incomplete, and possibly incorrect, an econometrics that was forced to use such theories as the only permissible
starting-point for data analysis could contribute no useful knowledge, except perhaps rejecting the theories. When
invariant features of reality exist, progressive research can discover them in part without prior knowledge of the whole.
Thus, Keynes's requirement of a complete theoretical speciﬁcation prior to data analysis is not necessary (see Hendry,
1995b). Indeed, a sequence of mutually encompassing LDGPs can be visualized, each of which is a valid
representation of the phenomena under analysis. Should no invariant features of reality exist, neither theories nor
econometric models would be of much practical value, even if the former could still produce abstract generalities of
the form commended by Robbins (1932).
A similar analysis applies to the attack by Koopmans on the study by Burns and
                                  EPILOGUE: THE SUCCESS OF GENERAL-TO-SPECIFIC                                          475


Mitchell. To rationalize Koopmans' belief that economics was already at a ‘Newtonian stage’, we require the (unstated)
assumption that only one sort of economic theory is applicable, that it is correct, and that it is immutable (see Hendry
and Morgan, 1995). Yet economic theory was progressing rapidly at the time (and still is), radically altering its views,
while being the subject of considerable dissension (as now). Koopmans correctly stressed that structural relations were
hidden behind observed regularities and needed to be prised out, requiring strong assumptions. But he then concluded
that ‘without resort to theory, in the sense indicated, conclusions relevant to the guidance of economic policies cannot
be drawn’. Such an argument may seem reasonable when backed by physics analogies, but is not sustainable in general.
Drawing on biochemistry for a counterexample, aspirin is perhaps the most common scientiﬁc intervention in
everyday life as a painkiller. The initial use of aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) arose as a folklore remedy for hangovers,
based on brewing willow-tree bark – of which it is a natural constituent; but until recently there was no rigorous theory
as to how aspirin cured headaches (see Weissmann, 1991). That did not stop it from working: policy-relevant
conclusions were easily drawn despite the absence of theory. More recently, and still without theoretical foundations,
aspirin has also come to be used to reduce heart problems.
Theories may be distinguished in terms of their levels: low-level theories are well established and widely accepted (e.g.
the optical theory of telescopes), whereas high-level theories assume the validity of lower levels and are subject to
doubt (as in theories of the accelerating expansion of the universe). Facts are items of empirical information which
depend only on low-level theories and measurements, and can be reliably replicated. All empirical evidence is theory-
laden to some degree, so ‘measurement without theory’ is impossible and must relate to the level of the theories used.
Thus, the appropriate blend of theory and empirical evidence is an issue of research efﬁciency, not validity.


2.7 ‘Lack of Identication’
As so often in debates, confusion is enhanced by imprecise deﬁnitions and concepts. ‘Identiﬁcation’ has several
possible attributes (as discussed in Hendry, 1997), namely ‘uniqueness’, ‘satisfying the required interpretation’, and
‘correspondence to the desired entity’. First, a non-unique result is clearly not identiﬁed, so the ﬁrst attribute is
necessary, as the discussion by Koopmans, Rubin and Leipnik (1950) of conditions for the uniqueness of coefﬁcients
in simultaneous systems makes clear. However, it is insufﬁcient, since uniqueness can be achieved by arbitrary
restrictions (criticized by Sims, 1980, inter alia). Secondly, there may exist a unique combination of several relationships
that is certain to be found in a given context, but then be incorrectly interpreted as one of those equations: for
example, a mix of supply and demand forces in a reduced form that has a positive price effect, but is wrongly
interpreted as a supply relation. Finally, a unique, interpretable model of a money-demand relation may in fact
correspond to a Central Bank's supply schedule, and this too is sometimes called ‘a failure to identify the demand
relation’.
Because the economy is highly interdependent, simultaneity was long believed to be a serious problem, inducing
spurious relations unless an a priori theory clariﬁed
476                                         RETROSPECT AND PROSPECT


in advance what connections should exist. Higher frequencies of observation have attenuated, but not eliminated, such
a uniqueness problem. However, simultaneity is not invariant under linear transformations – although linear systems
are – and is easily avoided by eschewing contemporaneous regressors until weak exogeneity is established.
Conditioning ensures a unique outcome, but it cannot guarantee that the resulting model corresponds to the
underlying reality.
A substantial role for ‘rational expectations’ might also pose problems when no expectations data are available, but its
extreme informational and processing assumptions suggest it has little empirical relevance (see e.g. Pesaran, 1987;
Hendry, 2000). Fortunately, the regular occurrence of structural breaks highlights mis-matches between models and
their corresponding LDGPs, so progressive research helps ensure their convergence.


2.8 Implications
The upshot of these attacks on empirical research was that almost all econometric studies had to commence from pre-
speciﬁed models (or pretend they did). Summers (1991) failed to notice that this was the source of his claimed
‘scientiﬁc illusion’: econometric evidence had become theory-dependent, with little value added, and a strong
propensity to be discarded when fashions in theory changed. Much empirical evidence depends only on low-level
theories which are part of the background knowledge base – not subject to scrutiny in the current analysis – so a data-
based approach to studying the economy is feasible. Since theory dependence has at least as many drawbacks as
sample dependence, data-modelling procedures are essential (see Hendry, 1995a).
We conclude that every criticism of Gets can be refuted. At the theoretical level, White (1990) showed that, with
sufﬁciently rigorous testing, the selected model will converge to the DGP. Thus, ‘overﬁtting’ (and mis-speciﬁcation)
problems are primarily ﬁnite sample. Moreover, Mayo (1981) emphasized that diagnostic test information is effectively
independent of the sufﬁcient statistics from which parameter estimates are derived. Thus, there is theoretical support
for a Gets approach. We will now consider some of the main developments that sustain this more positive view that
Gets will also accurately locate a congruent encompassing approximation to the LDGP, commencing with the
developments in Hoover and Perez (1999).


3 Methodological Innovations
In the course of their evaluation of general-to-speciﬁc methods, Hoover and Perez (1999) introduce ﬁve important
innovations potentially relevant to every empirical modelling approach. These developments arose from the exigencies
of programming Gets in order to conduct Monte Carlo simulations of its properties. Nevertheless, their applicability
extends well beyond ensuring that the algorithm is operational.2
Their ﬁrst innovation is to search many different reduction paths from the general unrestricted model (GUM), not just
the path given by eliminating variables in order from the smallest t-value upwards. Each search path is terminated
either when there
                                  EPILOGUE: THE SUCCESS OF GENERAL-TO-SPECIFIC                                          477


are no further feasible reductions (e.g. all remaining variables satisfy the simpliﬁcation criterion, perhaps | t| > 2) or
when a deletion induces a signiﬁcant diagnostic test outcome. The models resulting from each search path are stored
for later analysis. The advantage of this development is that any single choice could get ‘stuck’ in a path that initially
deleted a variable that really mattered in the DGP, thereby retaining many other variables as proxies, and hence ending
with non-parsimonious, incorrect, selections. Other paths help avoid that ‘mistake’; so when combined, they produce
selections which are both more parsimonious and less mis-speciﬁed.
The second innovation is simply to ensure that the algorithm undertakes only reductions which leave diagnostic tests
insigniﬁcant. This is essential to retain congruence and is always an integral part of the recommended approach, but
many search procedures fail to implement such a check. Moreover, Hoover and Perez are then able to investigate the
interaction of variable selection and diagnostic testing. This has eluded most attempts at theoretical analysis, and
although Monte Carlo is always problem-dependent, their ﬁndings cohere with what theory exists. Since the null is
true, any diagnostic checking acts as a constraint on reduction, so must increase the overall ‘size’ of the selection
process (in terms of retaining spurious variables). Thus, the choice of which – and how many – diagnostic tests to
compute is important if a search is to progress towards simpliﬁcation. It is also essential to ensure that the selected
tests have the correct size, with a relatively small size for each (e.g. 1 per cent when tests for residual autocorrelation,
non-normality, non-constancy, and heteroscedasticity are all used) to keep the overall null-rejection frequency low.
Present approaches to diagnostic testing emphasize power to detect mis-speciﬁcation, so may veer towards over-
selection. Conversely, by checking diagnostically at every stage, false deletions can be detected, so the ﬁnal selection of
the relevant variables could end closer to the DGP. Moreover, by ensuring congruence, the conventional standard
errors used at every step are consistent estimators, and so valid inferences are sustained.
Of course, by searching several paths, a number of distinct (non-nested) models might be found. This leads to their
third innovation: the suggestion of using encompassing tests to select between the contenders generated by alternative
paths from a common initial model. (Hoover and Perez actually select the best-ﬁtting model in their recorded
outcomes, but they cite the encompassing principle.) As a result, either there will be a unique encompassing selection,
or if several mutually encompassing models remain, one can be selected by an information criterion. Consequently,
despite there being many searches, a unique outcome is guaranteed; and by conducting diagnostic tests at every search
stage, with a path terminated only if every feasible deletion induces an insigniﬁcant diagnostic test value, the ﬁnal
selection is bound to be congruent, and hence must parsimoniously encompass the initial model. This role of
encompassing in selecting between models resulting from different search paths has not been studied previously:
despite working on both the Gets approach and encompassing for many years, it is also an idea that I completely
missed, even though rival models could easily be construed in that way. With hindsight, encompassing is probably an
important aspect in ‘controlling’ the overall size of a Gets selection process given the many paths searched, entailing
perhaps hundreds of tests.
The fourth innovation of Hoover and Perez is the use of sub-samples to reﬁne the
478                                           RETROSPECT AND PROSPECT


selection of variables (as distinct from testing constancy). Of course, recursive estimation has long been in the core of
the Gets research programme; but it was oriented towards checking constancy, whereas their insight is to use the same
information to determine overall signiﬁcance. Since a central t-test wanders around the origin, the probability is low
that an effect which is signiﬁcant only by chance in the full sample will also be signiﬁcant in two independent sub-
samples. Conversely, a non-central t-test diverges, so should be signiﬁcant in both sub-samples, perhaps at a lower level
of signiﬁcance to reﬂect the use of smaller samples. Hoover and Perez use over-lapping samples, but the logic
generalizes, and an appropriate probability analysis is presented in Hendry and Krolzig (2000). The idea works well in
their Monte Carlo, and suggests the possibility of reducing ‘overﬁtting’ relative to their original algorithm: it should be a
particularly powerful strategy for model selection when breaks occur in some of the marginal relations over either of
the sub-samples.
Fifthly, Hoover and Perez clarify various categories of ‘success’ and ‘failure’ in addition to the success of precisely
locating the DGP. This is an important reﬁnement relative to Lovell, and helps reveal which models are selected when
‘incorrect’ choices are made. They sensibly refer to the algorithm failing (rather than the methodology): improvements
in the algorithm could alter the simulation outcomes without changing the methodology, and do so in Hendry and
Krolzig (1999b). Some investigators might regard their category 2 (retaining the DGP variables plus some others) as
the worst kind of failure, by spurious overﬁtting; whereas others would condemn the inability of the search procedure
to detect effects that might be of policy signiﬁcance. Neither type of error is inherent in the methodology per se, or the
algorithm, but can be selected by the choices of critical values at the many stages involved in the search process. In our
re-run of these experiments, lowering the signiﬁcance levels of the diagnostic tests from (say) 0.05 to 0.01 reduced the
overall selection size noticeably (owing to the difference in powering up 0.95 and 0.99 repeatedly), without greatly
affecting the power of the model-selection procedure. However, it must be remembered that the diagnostics simply
acted as constraints on simpliﬁcation in such experiments, since the errors were well behaved, and there must be
corresponding power losses in detecting error mis-speciﬁcations. Increasing the signiﬁcance levels of the selection t-
tests also reduces the empirical size, but lowers the power more noticeably for variables with population t-values
smaller than 3. This trade-off is therefore selectable by an investigator. Consequently, whether or not the ‘LSE’
approach over- or under-selects is not intrinsic to it, but depends on how it is used. The advocacy of smaller
signiﬁcance levels (1 per cent versus 5 per cent) for diagnostic tests probably has much to commend it; section 7
comments on selection-test signiﬁcance levels.
To investigate how well such an algorithm worked, Hoover and Perez re-ran the experiments in Lovell (1983), who
had sought to evaluate the ability of some ‘model-selection methods’ to locate a single conditional equation (with from
zero to ﬁve regressors) from a large macroeconomic database (containing up to forty variables once lags were
included). As noted above, Lovell found that none of the methods worked very well, inducing a belief in the
economics profession that ‘data mining’ was best avoided. Although the Lovell database implicitly embodies many
‘hidden’ relations between variables as in real economies, and is of a scale and complexity
                                   EPILOGUE: THE SUCCESS OF GENERAL-TO-SPECIFIC                                            479


that can occur in empirical macroeconomics, beginning with forty regressors and hoping to select precisely the correct
subset of causal variables by statistical criteria is incredibly optimistic. Moreover, it is far from what was advised in this
book, as such an approach completely ignores the information available from economic analysis and fails to transform
to a near-orthogonal parameterization. Finally, none of the methods simulated by Lovell approaches the structured
nature of Gets, and hence earlier poor ﬁndings have no implications for how well Gets might perform when embodied
in an algorithm that fully implements the methodology.
We next dispose of a potential criticism of their simulation procedure (not of their algorithm). Hoover and Perez start
with highly over-parameterized models which nest the DGP, and conduct mis-speciﬁcation tests for their congruence:
since the null hypotheses are correct, all rejections are chance. However, some rejections will occur, leading to the
initial model (and the DGP) being rejected. This must also be a feature of empirical studies, unless an investigator
knew the truth, and knew that she knew it, so no mis-speciﬁcation tests were needed. Such samples are aberrant, but in
a non-replicable world one would tentatively conclude that their features were aspects of the DGP. Thus, either the test
size must be reduced – so the decision becomes one of not rejecting – or the starting-point re-speciﬁed to remove the
problem (Hoover and Perez omit samples where several diagnostic test rejections occur). In Monte Carlo, the former
seems the feasible solution; empirically the latter will usually occur, so a study of the consequences of doing so needs to
be undertaken.
In these experiments, one variable (yt) is generated by simulation as a function of the observed values (xi,t, i = 1, . . . , k)
of a few other database variables (k = 0, . . . , 5) with parameter vector β, plus a set of random numbers {εt}:




                                                                                                                         (20.3)
Since all the {xi,t} are held ﬁxed across replications, and the error processes are mutually and serially independent, they
are strongly exogenous for β (see Engle, Hendry and Richard, 1983). Then the generated {yt} is regressed on all the
database variables plus their lags, commencing from the GUM:




                                                                                                                         (20.4)
The ‘methodology’ is tested by seeing how often (20.3) is found when commencing from (20.4). In most experiments
it performed admirably – and where it did less well, reﬁnements to the algorithm are feasible to improve its behaviour,
without changing the methodology, as we now discuss.


4 Improving the Algorithm
The most important long-run contribution of Hoover and Perez (1999) may be that it also opened the door to a range
of important enhancements to their ‘baseline’ algorithm. We ﬁrst reﬁne the important distinction between the costs of
inference
480                                            RETROSPECT AND PROSPECT


and the costs of search, and then consider some feasible improvements to the search process.


4.1 Costs of Inference and Costs of Search
The distinction between the costs of inference and those of search is essential to clarify the notion of the ‘success’ of a
search algorithm as discussed in section 2.4. Judging a search procedure by whether or not it exactly locates the DGP
implicitly entails a baseline where the truth is known, and the investigator is certain that it is the truth. Rather, to isolate
the costs of selection, we judge its retention and deletion probabilities against the same procedures applied to testing
the DGP. For example, in each replication of a Monte Carlo simulation experiment, both the correct DGP model and
the GUM are ﬁtted, and the same selection criteria applied: one then evaluates the selection rates for the causal
variables when commencing from the GUM with the selection rates when no search is needed (i.e. inference is
conducted once for each causal variable in the DGP), and adds any additional (non-causal) variables that are retained.
Let        denote the probability of retaining the ith variable when commencing from the DGP using a selection test
sequence with signiﬁcance level α. Then            is the cost of inference. Let    denote the probability of retaining the
ith variable when commencing from the GUM, also using signiﬁcance level α. Then pure search costs are                        .
For irrelevant variables,       , so the whole cost of retaining adventitiously signiﬁcant variables is attributed to search,
plus any additional costs for failing to retain relevant variables. The former can be lowered by increasing the
signiﬁcance levels of selection tests, but at the cost of reducing the latter. However, it is feasible to lower size and raise
power simultaneously by an improved search algorithm.


4.2 Improvements Embodied in PcGets
First, PcGets undertakes ‘pre-search’ simpliﬁcation F-tests to exclude variables from the GUM, after which the GUM is
reformulated. Since variables found to be irrelevant on such tests are excluded from later analyses, this step uses a
loose signiﬁcance level (such as 75 per cent or 50 per cent). Such a high value might seem surprising given the
argument that selection leads to over-parameterization, but it conﬁrms that such claims are not sustainable. We return
to this issue in section 7 below.
Secondly, diagnostic tests of the GUM will be signiﬁcant by chance with an average frequency determined by the pre-
selected level under the null. Empirical investigators would undoubtedly re-specify the GUM in such a case, since they
cannot discriminate between rejection due to high power and to type-I errors. In the absence of such re-speciﬁcation,
to proceed down any reduction path our algorithm must raise the required signiﬁcance level of diagnostic tests which
reject, and so terminates search paths only when that new level is violated (Hoover and Perez drop such tests from the
checking set, so an ever-increasing problem of that type could lurk undetected).
Block tests also constitute feasible search paths, in addition to individual-coefﬁcient
                                 EPILOGUE: THE SUCCESS OF GENERAL-TO-SPECIFIC                                          481


tests. Both theory and practical experience to date suggest that block tests produce more parsimonious ﬁnal selections
yet have a higher probability of retaining relevant variables.
Thirdly, after the initial selection of simpliﬁed models from the GUM, formal encompassing tests between the
contenders eliminate those which are dominated but do not dominate any other model. If a unique choice does not
result, then we form the union of the resulting models, which becomes a new starting-point for path searches. The
algorithm repeats until the union is unchanged between successive rounds. The ﬁnal model, if it is not already unique,
is selected by an information criterion (such as BIC: see Schwarz, 1978).
Fourthly, for that unique ﬁnal model, the sub-sample reliability of its coefﬁcients is evaluated by the proposal in
Hoover and Perez for overlapping split-sample checks. The algorithm then concludes that some variables are deﬁnitely
excluded (those not in the ﬁnal model); some are deﬁnitely included (these satisfy the selection criterion in the ﬁnal
model and both sub-samples); and some have an uncertain role, varying from a reliability of zero (e.g. included in the
ﬁnal model, but insigniﬁcant – probably because deleting it induces a signiﬁcant diagnostic – and insigniﬁcant in both
sub-samples), through to an upper bound pre-set by the user (signiﬁcant overall and in one sub-sample). Investigators
are at liberty to interpret such evidence as they see ﬁt, noting that further simpliﬁcation of the selected congruent
model will induce some violations of congruence or encompassing.


4.3 Integrated Variables
To date, PcGets conducts all inferences as if the data were not integrated (denoted |(0)). Almost all selection tests
remain valid even when the data are integrated of order one (|(1)), since only t- or F-tests for an effect that
corresponds to a unit root require non-standard critical values (see Sims, Stock and Watson, 1990). The empirical
examples on |(1) data provided in section 8 below do not reveal any problems, but in principle it might be useful to
implement cointegration tests and appropriate differencing transformations as initial reductions. Further, Wooldridge
(1999) proves that mis-speciﬁcation tests of the GUM are valid even for integrated time series, and we presume that
this also holds for simpliﬁcations thereof.


4.4 Specifying the GUM
The starting-point for Gets model selection is the general unrestricted model, so the key issues concern its speciﬁcation
and congruence. The larger the initial regressor set, the more likely it is that adventitious effects will be retained; but
the smaller the GUM, the more likely that key variables will be omitted. Further, the less orthogonality between
variables, the more ‘confusion’ the algorithm faces, leading to a proliferation of mutually encompassing models, where
ﬁnal choices may differ only marginally (e.g. lag 2 versus 1). Finally, the initial speciﬁcation must be congruent, with no
mis-speciﬁcation tests failed at the outset. Empirically, the GUM would be revised if such tests rejected, and little is
known about the consequences of doing so (although PcGets will enable such studies in the near future). As noted, in
Monte
482                                           RETROSPECT AND PROSPECT


Carlo experiments, the program automatically changes the signiﬁcance levels of diagnostic tests following rejections on
the GUM.
Davidson and Hendry (1981: 257) mentioned four main problems in the general-to-speciﬁc methodology: (i) the
chosen ‘general’ model can be inadequate, comprising too special a case of the LDGP; (ii) data limitations may
preclude specifying the desired relation; (iii) the non-existence of an optimal sequence for simpliﬁcation leaves open the
choice of reduction path; and (iv) potentially large type-II error probabilities of the individual tests may be needed to
avoid a high type-I error of the overall sequence. By adopting the ‘multiple path’ development of Hoover and Perez
(1999) and implementing a range of important improvements, PcGets overcomes the problems associated with points
(iii) and (iv). However, the empirical success of PcGets must depend crucially on the creativity of each researcher in
specifying the general model, and the feasibility of estimating it from the available data – aspects beyond the capabilities
of the program, other than the diagnostic tests serving their usual role of revealing model mis-speciﬁcation.
There is a central role for economic theory in the modelling process in ‘prior speciﬁcation’, ‘prior simpliﬁcation’, and
suggesting admissible data transforms. The ﬁrst of these relates to the inclusion of potentially relevant variables, the
second to the exclusion of irrelevant effects, and the third to the appropriate formulations in which the inﬂuences to be
included are entered, such as log or ratio transforms etc., differences and cointegration vectors, and any likely linear
transformations that might enhance orthogonality between regressors. The ‘LSE approach’ argued for a close link of
theory and model, and explicitly opposed ‘running regressions on every variable in the database’ as in Lovell (1983)
(see e.g. Hendry and Ericsson, 1991a). Unfortunately, economic theory often provides no basis for specifying the lag
lengths in empirical macro-models: even when a theoretical model is dynamic, a ‘time period’ is usually not well
deﬁned. In practice, lags are chosen either for analytical convenience (e.g. ﬁrst-order differential equation systems) or
to allow for some desirable features (as in the choice of a linear, second-order difference equation to replicate cycles).
Therefore, we adopt the approach of starting with an unrestricted autoregressive-distributed lag model with a maximal
lag length set according to available evidence (e.g. as four or ﬁve for quarterly time series, to allow for seasonal
dynamics). Prior analysis remains essential for appropriate parameterizations, functional forms, choice of variables, lag
lengths, and indicator variables (including seasonals, special events, etc.). Orthogonalization helps notably in selecting a
unique representation, as does validly reducing the initial GUM. It is to be hoped that automating the reduction
process will enable researchers to concentrate their efforts on designing the GUM, which could signiﬁcantly improve
the empirical success of the algorithm.


4.5 Stages of PcGets
Building on the developments just described, the ‘testimation’ process of PcGets depends on the choice of:
  •     the n diagnostic checks in the test battery;
  •     the parameters of these diagnostic tests;
                                  EPILOGUE: THE SUCCESS OF GENERAL-TO-SPECIFIC                                            483


  •     the signiﬁcance levels η of the n diagnostics;
  •     pre-search F-test simpliﬁcations;
  •     the signiﬁcance levels δ of such tests;
  •     the simpliﬁcation tests (t and/or F);
  •     the signiﬁcance levels α of the simpliﬁcation tests;
  •     the signiﬁcance levels γ of the encompassing tests;
  •     the sub-sample split;
  •     the signiﬁcance levels κ of the sub-sample tests.
PcGets allows users to set as options: the choices of diagnostic and selection tests, the signiﬁcance levels for diagnostic
tests, pre-selection tests, block F-tests, t-test selections, encompassing tests, and split-sample tests, as well as the ﬁnal-
model selection criterion, and the percentage overlap in the sub-sample split. Then PcGets simply implements all the
principles discussed in earlier chapters: given a congruent general dynamic statistical model, selection tests eliminate
statistically insigniﬁcant variables, diagnostic checks ensure a congruent ﬁnal model, encompassing resolves model
choice, and sub-sample tests help eliminate ‘spuriously signiﬁcant’ regressors. Both its Monte Carlo success in locating
the DGP and its empirical behaviour for the DHSY and UK M1 data sets conﬁrm the power of this operational
version of the methodology.
Each of the above stages is susceptible to analysis conditional on reaching that stage; and some combinations of steps
can be formalized (e.g. one round of selection together with diagnostic testing); but the complex interactions between
all the stages have eluded analysis to date. Moreover, forced search paths can be implemented, so an investigator can
study the best model which can be selected subject to ensuring the presence of a subset of the variables, perhaps of
major interest theoretically. The next two sections consider the probabilities of selecting relevant, and deleting
irrelevant, variables, respectively. Using the ‘conventional’ approaches described above, the outlook seems bleak, but
section 7 suggests that substantial improvements are feasible.


5 Selection Probabilities
One might hardly expect a search algorithm to do better than the same principles of testing applied to the DGP. When
searching a large database for that DGP, an investigator could well retain the relevant regressors much less often than
when the correct speciﬁcation is known, in addition to retaining irrelevant variables in the ﬁnally selected model. We
ﬁrst examine the problem of retaining signiﬁcant variables commencing from the DGP, then turn to any additional
power losses resulting from search.
For a regression coefﬁcient βi, hypothesis tests of the null H0: βi = 0 will reject with a probability dependent on the non-
centrality parameter of the test. We consider the slightly more general setting where t-tests are used to check an
hypothesis, denoted t(n, ψ) for n degrees of freedom, when ψ is the non-centrality parameter, equal to zero under the
null. For a critical value cα, P(| t| ≥ cα | H0) = α, where H0 implies ψ = 0. The following table records some
approximate power calculations when one
484                                           RETROSPECT AND PROSPECT


coefﬁcient null hypothesis is tested and when four are tested, in each case, precisely once.
   t-test powers
   ψ                       n                       α                       P(| t| ≥ cα)            P(| t| ≥ cα)4
   1                       100                     0.05                    0.16                    0.001
   2                       50                      0.05                    0.50                    0.063
   2                       100                     0.01                    0.26                    0.005
   3                       50                      0.01                    0.64                    0.168
   4                       50                      0.05                    0.98                    0.902
   4                       50                      0.01                    0.91                    0.686
   6                       50                      0.01                    1.00                    0.997

Thus, there is little hope of retaining variables with ψ = 1, and only a 50:50 chance of retaining a single variable with a
theoretical | t| of 2 when the critical value is also 2, falling to 30:70 for a critical value of 2.6. When ψ = 3, the power
of detection is sharply higher, but still leads to more than 35 per cent mis-classiﬁcations. Finally, when ψ = 4, one such
variable will almost always be retained.
However, the ﬁnal column shows that the probability of retaining all four relevant variables with the given non-
centrality is essentially negligible even when they are independent, except in the last few cases. Mixed cases (with
different values of ψ) can be calculated by multiplying the probabilities in the fourth column (e.g. for ψ = 2, 3, 4, 6 the
joint P(·) = 0.15 at α = 0.01). Such combined probabilities are highly nonlinear in ψ, since one is almost certain to
retain all four when ψ = 6, even at a 1 per cent signiﬁcance level. The important conclusion is that, despite ‘knowing’
the DGP, low signal-noise variables will rarely be retained using t-tests when there is any need to test the null; and if
there are many relevant variables, it is unlikely that all of them will be retained even when they have quite large non-
centralities.


6 Deletion Probabilities
The most extreme case where low deletion probabilities might entail high search costs is when many variables are
included but none actually matters. PcGets systematically checks the reducibility of the GUM by testing simpliﬁcations
up to the empty model. A one-off F-test FG of the GUM against the null model using critical value cγ would have size

retention rates of spuriously signiﬁcant variables.
Thus, in contrast to the relatively high costs of inference discussed in the previous section, those of search arising from
retaining additional irrelevant variables are almost negligible. For a reasonable GUM with say forty variables where
twenty-ﬁve are irrelevant, even without the pre-selection and multiple path searches of PcGets, and using just t-tests at 5
per cent, roughly one spuriously signiﬁcant variable will be retained by chance. Against that, from the previous section,
there is at most a 50 percent chance of retaining each of the variables that have non-centralities less than 2, and little
chance of keeping them all. It should now be clear than the difﬁcult problem is retention of relevance, not elimination
of irrelevance. The only two solutions are better inference procedures and looser critical values; we will consider them
both.

8 Applying PcGets
Simulation and empirical applications differ in the key feature that the model nests the DGP in the former, but the
relation between model and LDGP is unknown in the latter. Considerable Monte Carlo evidence on the behaviour of
PcGets is presented in Hendry and Krolzig (1999b) and Krolzig and Hendry (2000), so we focus here on the two
central modelling examples of this book, namely UK consumers' expenditure following Davidson, Hendry, Srba and
Yeo (1978) (denoted by the acronym DHSY) and UK narrow money demand. Although the ‘truth’ values of the
results cannot be established, a question of interest is whether the selected model matches, or even beats, that
developed by the earlier authors.

9 Conclusion
We have demonstrated that the performance of the ﬁrst mechanized general-to-speciﬁc algorithms is excellent; yet
these represent early attempts at computer automation. Moving from the relatively poor performance of every method
considered by
490                                             RETROSPECT AND PROSPECT


Lovell (1983), Hoover and Perez (1999) achieved signiﬁcant progress towards a viable algorithm, and PcGets has
already shown that further improvements in design can induce markedly better selection behaviour. For example,
when the null model is true but the GUM includes more than forty variables, simplistic search procedures such as
step-wise regression will ﬁnd it under 20 per cent of the time: yet re-running the Lovell simulation experiments,
Hoover and Perez (1999) found it in almost 80 per cent of trials at a 1 per cent signiﬁcance level, as against 97 per cent
using the pre-release version of PcGets reported in Hendry and Krolzig (1999b). A bright future awaits.
The speciﬁcation of a congruent general unrestricted model remains central to the performance of the search process,
but the low costs of search found here, and by Hoover and Perez, suggest adopting relatively generous
parameterizations in the GUM. The less the orthogonality between variables, the more ‘confusion’ the algorithm faces,
which can lead to a proliferation of mutually encompassing models, where the ﬁnal choice may differ only marginally
(e.g. lag 2 versus 1). Careful prior analysis therefore remains essential, concerning the parameterization, functional
form, choice of variables, lag length, indicators and so on. By greatly reducing the effort needed to develop simpliﬁed
ﬁnal selections, PcGets should allow much more ‘thinking’ time to relate the economic analysis to the data. Moreover,
the requirement to return to the GUM and not simply patch a model when an extension is required becomes much
less daunting when a few seconds' computation can deliver a viable reduction.
The thrust of the analysis to date has been for single-equation, conditional models precisely because even in that
context ‘data mining’ in the widest sense has been thought to be a serious problem. Applying the methodology
advocated in earlier chapters in a structured search procedure conclusively refutes that belief. Just as the original
approaches were ﬁrst essayed on the simplest class of models before multi-variable extensions could be sensibly
developed, so too with search algorithms. Direct extensions to modelling cointegrated vector autoregressions are easily
envisaged, and selection procedures using instrumental variables rather than least squares are already operational. A
maximum likelihood generalization is also straightforward to imagine, though perhaps harder to implement, although
special cases such as limited dependent variables should not pose any great difﬁculties. Cross-section data can already
be handled, and panels will undoubtedly follow shortly.
The prospects for empirical econometric modelling are as exciting today as I have ever seen – the best imaginable note
on which to conclude this book.
